abstract: The linear ubiquitin chain assembly complex (LUBAC) is a critical regulator of tumor necrosis factor (TNF) signaling that promotes pro-survival responses and suppresses apoptosis. Linear ubiquitination of the TNFR1-associated complex II components FADD and Caspase-8 has been reported, but whether they are direct LUBAC substrates, how they are modified, and what the modification does remain poorly understood. Here, we show that loss of HOIP, which destabilizes the LUBAC complex, sensitizes HCT116 cells to TNF-induced apoptosis, and that TNF induces linear ubiquitin-reactive species on endogenous FADD and Caspase-8. Using purified proteins, we demonstrate that FADD and Caspase-8 are direct LUBAC substrates with different catalytic requirements. Efficient FADD ubiquitination requires HOIL-1L in addition to HOIP, consistent with a priming-and-extension mechanism, whereas Caspase-8 is ubiquitinated by HOIP-containing subcomplexes lacking HOIL-1L. A complex containing FADD, Caspase-8, and RIPK1 formed independently of LUBAC activity, but pharmacological inhibition of HOIP increased Caspase-8 processing within the FADD-associated pool, and Met1-ubiquitinated FADD showed reduced binding to Caspase-8 in vitro. Mapping identified four death domain lysines that each support LUBAC-dependent FADD ubiquitination. In FADD-deficient cells, a FADD-diubiquitin fusion attenuated TNF/cycloheximide-induced apoptosis relative to wild-type FADD, whereas a lysine-less FADD supported apoptosis with delayed kinetics. Together, these findings identify FADD and Caspase-8 as direct LUBAC substrates modified through distinct catalytic routes and support a model in which ubiquitination of FADD limits productive engagement with Caspase-8.
